---
title: "Derivatives"
subtitle: "ConvolutionInterpolations.jl against Interpolations.jl, BSplineKit.jl and Dierckx.jl"
engine: julia
---

The first three derivatives of a difficult function from uniformly spaced samples: the
analytic derivatives of the convolution kernels against those of the cubic B-spline of
Interpolations.jl (first and second only, which is what it offers), the B-spline interpolants
of BSplineKit.jl, and the quintic FITPACK spline of Dierckx.jl. First the accuracy as the grid
is refined, then the time to evaluate a first derivative, and finally the time each method
needs to reach a given accuracy in it.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Packages, the methods, and the test function"
using ConvolutionInterpolations
import Interpolations                # qualified: exports `interpolate`, as BSplineKit does
import BSplineKit
import Dierckx
using Chairmarks, Printf, Random, CairoMakie

runge(x) = 1 / (1 + 25x^2)                                # Runge's function
function drunge(x, m)                                     # its m-th derivative, m = 1, 2, 3
    s = 1 + 25x^2
    m == 1 ? -50x / s^2 :
    m == 2 ? 50 * (75x^2 - 1) / s^3 :
             15000x * (1 - 25x^2) / s^4
end
xr = range(-1, 1, length = 2001)                          # fine points for measuring the error

# each method maps (x, y, m) to a callable m-th derivative, or `nothing` where it has none
function interpolations_derivative(x, y, m)
    m > 2 && return nothing                               # Interpolations.jl offers gradient and hessian
    s = Interpolations.scale(Interpolations.interpolate(y,
            Interpolations.BSpline(Interpolations.Cubic(Interpolations.Line(Interpolations.OnGrid())))), x)
    m == 1 ? (p -> Interpolations.gradient(s, p)[1]) : (p -> Interpolations.hessian(s, p)[1])
end
bsplinekit_derivative(k) = (x, y, m) -> begin
    S = BSplineKit.interpolate(x, y, BSplineKit.BSplineOrder(k))
    BSplineKit.Derivative(m) * S                          # the spline's m-th derivative, itself a spline
end
dierckx_derivative(x, y, m) = (spl = Dierckx.Spline1D(collect(x), collect(y); k = 5);
                               p -> Dierckx.derivative(spl, p; nu = m))
convinterp_derivative(kernel, maxm) = (x, y, m) ->
    m > maxm ? nothing : convolution_interpolation(x, y; kernel = kernel, derivative = m)

methods = [
    "Interpolations.jl cubic" => interpolations_derivative,
    "BSplineKit k=4"          => bsplinekit_derivative(4),
    "BSplineKit k=8"          => bsplinekit_derivative(8),
    "Dierckx k=5"             => dierckx_derivative,
    "ConvInterp :a4"          => convinterp_derivative(:a4, 1),
    "ConvInterp :b5"          => convinterp_derivative(:b5, 3),
    "ConvInterp :b7"          => convinterp_derivative(:b7, 5),
];
```

## Convergence

The largest error of each derivative against the exact one, as the number of samples doubles.
A method appears in a panel only if it provides that derivative order:

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "The convergence study"
ns = [41, 81, 161, 321, 641, 1281]
hs = 2 ./ (ns .- 1)
errs = Dict((name, m) => Float64[] for (name, _) in methods, m in 1:3)
for n in ns
    x = range(-1, 1, length = n)
    y = runge.(x)
    for (name, meth) in methods, m in 1:3
        d = meth(x, y, m)
        d === nothing && continue
        push!(errs[(name, m)], maximum(abs.(d.(xr) .- drunge.(xr, m))))
    end
end

fig = Figure(size = (800, 900))
axes = [Axis(fig[m, 1]; xscale = log10, yscale = log10, xreversed = true,
             title = "derivative order $m", xlabel = "spacing h", ylabel = "largest error") for m in 1:3]
for (name, _) in methods, m in 1:3
    isempty(errs[(name, m)]) && continue
    scatterlines!(axes[m], hs, max.(errs[(name, m)], 1e-17); markersize = 8, label = name)
end
for m in 1:3
    Legend(fig[m, 2], axes[m])                            # each panel lists the methods it has
end
fig
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
# the order over the last refinement that is clear of the method's floor: both of its errors at
# least ten times the error at the finest grid, so that a segment ending on the floor is never
# measured; for a method that has not reached a floor, the last refinement of the study
function observed(e)
    j = findlast(j -> e[j] > 10 * e[end], 2:length(e))
    j = j === nothing ? length(e) : j + 1
    log(e[j-1] / e[j]) / log(hs[j-1] / hs[j])
end
println("| observed order | derivative 1 | derivative 2 | derivative 3 |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|--:|")
for (name, _) in methods
    cells = [isempty(errs[(name, m)]) ? "—" : @sprintf("%.2f", observed(errs[(name, m)])) for m in 1:3]
    println("| ", name, " | ", join(cells, " | "), " |")
end
```

Every method loses about one order per derivative: the cubic B-spline of BSplineKit.jl from
4th order down to a piecewise-constant third derivative, Dierckx's quintic and `:b5` from 6th,
BSplineKit at order 8 and `:b7` from their interpolation order. The cubic of Interpolations.jl
is the exception at the second derivative: its boundary condition is the natural spline's,
which sets the second derivative to zero at the ends, so the largest error of that derivative
is at the boundary and does not fall with the grid. The rounding floor of a derivative rises with the
number of samples, as $1/h^m$, which is the price of differentiating sampled data and
the same for every method.

## Query time

Evaluation time per point of the first derivative, at a million random points on a grid of a
thousand samples, each derivative built once and evaluated in one broadcast:

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "The timings"
rng = MersenneTwister(1)
x1 = range(-1, 1, length = 1000)
y1 = runge.(x1)
p1 = rand(rng, 1_000_000) .* 1.98 .- 0.99

rows = map(methods) do (name, meth)
    d = meth(x1, y1, 1)
    t_query = (@b $d.($p1)).time / length(p1)
    (name = name, t_query = t_query)
end;
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
fmt(t) = t < 1e-6 ? @sprintf("%.0f ns", 1e9 * t) :
         t < 1e-3 ? @sprintf("%.1f μs", 1e6 * t) : @sprintf("%.2f ms", 1e3 * t)
println("| | first derivative, per point |")
println("|:--|--:|")
for r in rows
    println("| ", r.name, " | ", fmt(r.t_query), " |")
end
```

A derivative of a convolution interpolant is the same stencil sum with the differentiated
kernel's weights, so it costs what the interpolant costs. A spline derivative is a spline of
one degree lower, evaluated like any spline; Interpolations.jl's `gradient` assembles the
derivative from the B-spline's pieces at each call.

## Time to accuracy

As on the [interpolation page](interpolation.qmd): for each method and each grid of the
convergence study, the time to construct the first derivative and evaluate it at a hundred
thousand points, against its error on that grid.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "The work–precision study"
pw = rand(rng, 100_000) .* 1.98 .- 0.99                   # the evaluation workload
times = Dict(name => Float64[] for (name, _) in methods)
for n in ns
    x = range(-1, 1, length = n)
    y = runge.(x)
    for (name, meth) in methods
        push!(times[name], (@b begin d = $meth($x, $y, 1); d.($pw) end).time)
    end
end

fig = Figure(size = (800, 420))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xscale = log10, yscale = log10,
          xlabel = "time to construct and evaluate the first derivative at 10⁵ points [s]", ylabel = "largest error")
for (name, _) in methods
    scatterlines!(ax, times[name], max.(errs[(name, 1)], 1e-17); markersize = 8, label = name)
end
Legend(fig[1, 2], ax)
fig
```

The picture is the interpolation page's, one order down: the curves are nearly vertical, so
each method's position is its cost per point and its depth is what its order buys, and the
kernels are first to any accuracy of the derivative down to its rounding floor.
